Villers-la-Ville
vee-LAIR-lah-VEEL
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Brabant, founded 1146 by monks sent from Clairvaux; now one of the largest monastic ruins in Europe)
French villers, from Latin villare, a hamlet or farm settlement, with la ville, the town; the farm settlement that became a town.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Villers in Brabant was founded in 1146 by a party Bernard sent from Clairvaux, and grew into one of the greatest abbeys of the Low Countries, with a vast church, immense ranges and estates across Brabant. Suppressed in 1796, quarried, cut through by a railway and left to the woods, it is now among the largest and most photographed monastic ruins in Europe — a hundred metres of roofless nave with trees growing in the triforium. The ruin is the entry, and Scripture has a register for it that is neither triumph nor sentiment but lament. “Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste” (Isa 64:11) is a prayer, not a gloat; “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1) teaches a people how to grieve over what their own sin brought down. A Protestant looking at Villers may hold that its theology was wrong and still say those words over it, and he will be the better for doing so.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men; lamentation as expression of sorrow, cries of grief; and waste as desolate, destroyed, ruined.

expand to see more

RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; also, in the plural, the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or other work of men.

LAMENTATION, n. Expression of sorrow; cries of grief; the act of bewailing.

WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; stripped; as, the land is laid waste.

DESOLATION, n. The act of deserting or abandoning; destruction; a desolate state; gloominess; sadness.

MAGNIFICENT, a. Grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; displaying grandeur.

Key Scripture

Isa 64:11 — "Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste."

Lam 1:1 — "How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!"

Psa 74:7 — "They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name to the ground."

Psa 102:26 — "They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed:"

Modern Corruption

A great Brabant abbey of 1146, now among the largest monastic ruins in Europe: a ruin Scripture teaches us to lament rather than enjoy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lament. “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary, they have defiled by casting down the dwelling place of thy name” (Psa 74:7) is a psalm, which means God has given his people words for exactly this grief; and a Protestant who feels only vindication at a wrecked abbey has a harder heart than the Psalmist.

The live misuse is the romantic one — the ruin as scenery, photographed for its atmosphere by people with no interest in what it was for. That is its own kind of forgetting. “They shall perish, but thou shalt endure” (Psa 102:26) is the only comfort on offer, and it is addressed to God rather than to the building.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin villare, a farm settlement; Hebrew shamem (H8074), to be desolate; Hebrew chorbah (H2723), a waste place; Greek eremosis (G2050), desolation; Hebrew qinah (H7015), a lamentation.

expand to see more

Latin villare — a hamlet or farmstead; the commonest place-name element in northern France and Belgium.

Hebrew shamem (H8074) — to be desolate, stunned; the word carries both the ruin and the horror at it.

Hebrew chorbah (H2723) — a waste, a ruin; “all our pleasant things are laid waste” (Isa 64:11).

Hebrew qinah (H7015) — a dirge, lamentation; the form of the book of Lamentations.

Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; the New Testament's word for a sanctuary laid waste.

Usage

"“where our fathers praised thee” (Isa 64:11) — a prayer over a wrecked sanctuary."

"“how is she become as a widow!” (Lam 1:1) — grief taught to a people by God himself."

"“They shall perish, but thou shalt endure” (Psa 102:26) — the only durable comfort before a ruin."
